title: Equivalence partitioning in 4 steps
hook: Test one representative from each class, not every possible input.

steps.label: Define the rule
steps.detail: Example: an order quantity must be a whole number from 1 to 10.

steps.label: Group equivalent inputs
steps.detail: Classes: valid integers 1–10, integers below 1, integers above 10, and fractions.

steps.label: Choose sample values
steps.detail: Try 5, 0, 12 and 2.5: one representative from each class.

steps.label: Check expected results
steps.detail: Accept 5; reject the other inputs with appropriate validation.

takeaway: Sample each class; use boundary tests and risk-based tests as well.
caption:
Equivalence partitioning groups inputs expected to behave the same way. Instead of testing every value, choose a representative from each valid and invalid class.

Example: if an order quantity must be a whole number from 1 to 10, try 5 (valid), 0 (too low), 12 (too high) and 2.5 (not an integer).

Then use boundary value analysis to test the edges separately. Which other classes would you check?
